<reason>PRO opened with a solid regressivity and fiscal-crowding case, but CON reframed the decisive metric (share of income lost by fuel-dependent informal workers, not dollars captured by the rich) and pressed a sequencing point PRO never escaped: under the motion the price shock is certain on day one while compensation is contingent on delivery, indexing, and a budget that PRO admitted would "tighten." CON turned PRO's own "launch near-universal and tighten later" into evidence that targeting as written excludes the missing middle, and flipped PRO's Nigeria/Iran examples by pointing out they are removals-with-promised-cash, i.e., the motion being executed. PRO's best counter—that subsidies end in an uncompensated exit anyway—was real but undercut by PRO's concession that "compensation before the shock was never on the menu," and CON's answer that a visible fiscal bill can be phased slowly while prices stay predictable was adequate. PRO also had three clipped turns, a real execution cost. CON made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.1–B2.6: CON's first rebuttal caught PRO's "near-universal and tighten later" as a concession on the motion's word "targeted," reframed the sliver-of-a-sliver point as the dollars-vs-income-share error, and set up the day-versus-years timing gap that PRO never bridged.</best_rebuttal>
